value.overview: The Central American Pygmy-Owl (Glaucidium griseiceps) is a very small owl of humid tropical forests in Central America and northwestern South America. It is active mainly at night but may hunt and call during the day. Although secretive in the canopy, it may be located when small birds gather to mob it. The species is a year-round resident and is represented in Costa Rica chiefly in lowland and foothill forests on the Caribbean side.
value.classification: It belongs to the owl family Strigidae and the genus Glaucidium, which includes the pygmy-owls. Taxonomic treatments differ on whether several geographic forms are recognized as subspecies.
value.identification: This tiny owl has a rounded head, short tail, and generally brown to rufous upperparts. The crown is marked with small pale spots, while the underparts are pale with darker streaking or barring. Like other pygmy-owls, it has conspicuous false eye-spots on the back of the head. It is easily confused with other small Glaucidium owls, so range, elevation, habitat, plumage details, and especially its distinctive repeated hooting pattern are useful for identification.
value.rangeHabitat: The Central American Pygmy-Owl ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to northwestern Colombia, with additional populations reported in northwestern Ecuador. It occupies humid evergreen lowland and foothill forest, forest edges, secondary woodland, semi-open areas, and sometimes mature cacao plantations. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the lowlands and lower slopes, especially along the Caribbean slope, generally at elevations below about 800 meters, and is uncommon to locally fairly common.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; no regular long-distance migration is known. Individuals may make local movements in response to food and habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of this species remains poorly documented. It is reported to nest in natural cavities in trees or in old woodpecker holes, rather than constructing an open nest. Available records indicate clutches of about two to four eggs, with breeding observations concentrated in April and May in parts of its range. In Costa Rica, it is presumed to breed in suitable lowland and foothill forest, but detailed information on nesting dates, incubation, and parental care is limited.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is not fully documented, but it is believed to include large insects and other arthropods, small lizards, small birds, and small mammals. The owl usually hunts from a perch within dense foliage, making short, rapid flights to seize prey. It can forage during daylight as well as at night, although it is most often detected by its calls rather than seen.
value.behavior: The Central American Pygmy-Owl is usually encountered alone or in pairs and spends much of its time in the forest canopy or at its edges. It often remains concealed in dense vegetation. Its presence may be revealed when small birds mob it. The song consists of a series of clear, evenly spaced hoots, sometimes beginning with a shorter group of notes and followed by a longer sequence. It is most vocal in the morning and late afternoon, but may call at other times.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is generally considered stable, but precise population estimates and long-term trend data are limited.
